lines.text: In 1971, two dozen students were locked in a basement at Stanford. It became the most famous experiment in psychology.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy-one, two dozen students were locked in a basement at Stanford. It became the most famous experiment in psychology.

lines.text: You know the ending. Within days, ordinary students playing guards turned cruel. The study was shut down after six days.
The lesson seemed obvious. Put good people in a bad system, and they become monsters.
For almost fifty years, textbooks taught exactly that.
But in 2018, a French researcher went back into the archives. The tapes. The notes. The interviews.
lines.say: But in twenty eighteen, a French researcher went back into the archives. The tapes. The notes. The interviews.

lines.text: And the story started to crack.
On one recording, a staff member pushes a guard to be tougher. The guards weren't left alone. They were coached.
Then the prisoner whose breakdown made the study famous said something nobody expected.
He said he was faking. He wanted out, so he could study for his exams.
So was it all fake? Not quite. Some guards really did turn harsh. And the man who ran it defended it until he died.
The real lesson might be darker. People don't just become cruel on their own. They do it when someone in charge makes it clear that's what is expected.
Which raises a question about every famous experiment you were ever taught.
Next file: thirty-eight witnesses watched a crime and did nothing. That story isn't true either.
